books.title: The Knitting Circle
books.author: Hester Vane
books.blurb: A grieving widow joins the village knitting circle, and learns why her new village is so very quiet.
pages: After Walter died, the house in town grew too loud. The clocks, the neighbours, the kettle, the radio I could not bear to turn off because he had always left it on. So I sold it and bought a cottage in Hollins Ferry, where the lane ends at the river and the loudest thing at night is an owl. The estate agent called it the quietest village in the county. I took that as a kindness.

The circle found me in my first week. Three women at my gate with a basket of wool and a cake under a cloth. Mrs Thorne, tall and silver, did the talking. The Pruitt sisters, round as teapots, smiled in turn.

"Thursdays, in the chapel hall," said Mrs Thorne. "We knit for the village. Idle hands, Mrs Hale, and idle hearts." I had not knitted since I was a girl. I said yes before I could think of a reason not to.

The chapel hall smelled of lavender and paraffin. There were five chairs in a ring round the stove, and one of them always stayed empty. "Winifred's," said the younger Pruitt, patting it. "She'll be back." I didn't ask where Winifred had gone. In a new place you learn to let the old stories keep themselves. They gave me needles and a ball of soft brown wool, and Mrs Thorne guided my hands until the stitches came.

We knitted scarves. Always scarves, and each one for someone in particular. That first month it was for Mr Abley, the postman, who whistled. He whistled at every gate, the same jaunty bar of something, over and over. "Such a cold round he has," said Mrs Thorne, casting off. We wrapped it in brown paper and tied it with string. He wore it the next morning, striped green and gold, and thanked us warmly at the gate.

It was a week before I noticed he had stopped whistling. He still came at nine. He still smiled. But he came up the path in perfect silence, the scarf wound twice around his throat, and went away the same.

"He seems tired," I said on Thursday. "He seems content," said Mrs Thorne. "There's a difference, and it's a good one." Her needles never paused. The wool on them was red, for the bell-ringer.

The bell-ringer was a big laughing man who rang the hours as if he were cross with them. After his scarf, the bells rang softly, then not at all. The schoolmistress, who sang as she walked her pupils down to the river, got a blue one, and walked them after that without a note. Hollins Ferry was the quietest village in the county. I was beginning to understand how it stayed that way.

I told myself it was grief. Widows see shadows in everything; my sister had warned me. But on the fifth Thursday I arrived early, and the hall was not empty. Mrs Thorne sat alone by the stove, holding a finished scarf to her ear like a shell. Her eyes were shut. From the wool, very faintly, came a whistled bar of something jaunty, over and over. She heard the door, lowered it, and smiled at me.

That night I sat with my needles idle in my lap and thought about the empty chair. The next Thursday I pleaded a headache and left early, and did not go home. I crept round to the vestry window instead. The circle kept a tall cupboard there that was always locked. Tonight it stood open, and Mrs Thorne and the Pruitts were bending over something inside it, the way you would bend over a cot.

It was a woman. Or the shape of one, sitting upright on a chair, knitted from head to heel in every colour of every scarf. Green and gold at the lips. Red at the chest, where a laugh would sit. Blue at the throat, where a song would. Her face was a smooth, soft knit with no eyes yet. As I watched, she drew a breath, slow and woollen, like someone very nearly waking.

"Nearly, Winifred," Mrs Thorne whispered, stroking the knitted hand. "A whistle, a laugh, a song. You were always the liveliest of us. Only the voice left now, and the voice must be a good one."

The younger Pruitt turned towards the window, and I ducked into the nettles. "The new one has a lovely voice," she said. "Low and sad. She reads aloud at night, did you know? To her husband. Who isn't there."

I ran home with my heart going the way the bells used to. On my doorstep was a parcel in brown paper, tied with string. Inside was a scarf the grey of a winter river, knitted fine and close, with my initials worked in one corner. I did not put it on. I put it in the stove and watched it burn, and I swear the smoke went up the flue in the shape of a held breath.

Then I went back to the chapel hall with Walter's old pocket knife. They had gone home. The cupboard was locked, but the lock was older than I am. I found the loose end at Winifred's heel, and I pulled. She came undone the way a winter does, all at once and then slowly, and the hall filled with sound. A whistle. A peal. A song. They flew out of the door and over the village like starlings.

In the morning Mr Abley whistled at my gate. The bells rang nine, cross and loud. Down by the river the schoolmistress was singing. On Thursday I went to the hall, because not to go would have been an answer, and the circle smiled at me, all three of them, and Mrs Thorne put a ball of grey wool into my hands. "Never mind, dear," she said. "We have all winter."

That was in October. It is December now, and I am writing this down because I find I can no longer say it. I don't remember casting on. But each morning there is more of the scarf in my basket, grey as a winter river, fine and close, my initials in the corner. My hands knit it while I sleep. Tonight it is long enough to go twice around a throat. In the chapel hall, a chair is waiting.

books.title: A Baker's Dozen
books.author: Clara Wynn
books.blurb: Thirteen early mornings, one stubborn baker, and the grumpy heir of the mill that supplies her flour.
pages: The first morning, the flour is late. Hattie Lark has been up since three, as she has every morning for nine years, and by half past four the ovens are roaring, the bowls are empty, and there is still no cart from Ashcombe Mill. At ten to five it comes, and the man who climbs down is not old Mr Ashcombe. He is younger, taller, and scowling as if the dark itself owes him money.

"Edmund Ashcombe," he says, heaving a sack onto his shoulder. "My father's hip has finally given out. The carter's retired. So it's me." He drops the sack on her floor, a little harder than he needs to.

"You're late," says Hattie. "You're welcome," says Edmund. She gives him a cinnamon bun anyway, because she gives one to everyone who comes through her door before dawn. He eats it in two bites and doesn't say thank you.

The second morning, he is on time, and grumpier for it. The third, he informs her that her back step is crooked and someone will break an ankle. The fourth, he complains that the bun is too sweet. On the fifth morning he says nothing at all about the bun, but she notices that he eats it slowly, standing in the warm doorway, watching the first loaves come out of the oven.

The sixth morning, the flour is wrong. Hattie knows it the moment she plunges her hands in: too fine, too white, flat as chalk. "This isn't from your stones," she says. Edmund looks at the floor. "The old wheel's broken. I've been buying it in from the big mill in the city until I can get it fixed. It's cheaper. Nobody will know." Hattie holds up a pale, sulking loaf. "I'll know," she says.

He doesn't come in on the seventh morning. He leaves the sacks on the step, and she hears the cart rattle off before she can get the door open. She bakes with what she has. The bread is fine. It is perfectly fine, and it tastes of nothing, and she finds she is cross about that in a way that has very little to do with bread, and quite a lot to do with an empty doorway.

On the eighth morning she doesn't wait for the cart. She leaves her apprentice with the ovens, walks the two miles to Ashcombe Mill in the dark with a basket on her arm, and finds Edmund up to his knees in the millrace with a lantern in his teeth, wrestling a broken paddle. He looks up at her, astonished, and drops the lantern. She hands him a bun. "Show me," she says.

They work until the sky goes grey. She holds the lantern; he swears softly at the iron pins. She learns that he hated the city, the office, the numbers that belonged to other people. He learns that she burns the first batch of anything new, every time, on purpose. "For luck," she says. "For nerves," he says. She doesn't deny it. When the wheel finally groans and turns, they both cheer like children.

The ninth morning, the flour is right again: creamy, nutty, faintly freckled with bran. Hattie bakes a rye loaf, dark and sour and crackling, and hands Edmund the heel of it, still too hot to hold. He tears it, smells it, eats it. Then he is quiet for so long she thinks something is wrong. "That," he says at last, "tastes like being nine years old. My mother used to buy this. From your aunt, I suppose."

On the tenth morning he brings news with the flour, and it is bad. His father wants to sell the mill. A company from the city has made an offer: they'll keep the building for show, and send the flour by lorry from somewhere else entirely. "It makes sense," Edmund says, in the flat voice of a man repeating someone else's sums. "It doesn't," says Hattie. "Not to anyone who eats bread."

The eleventh morning, she is late for once. She has been up half the night, knocking on doors. The pub wants Ashcombe flour. So does the school, the tea room by the green, the two farm shops, and the vicar's wife, who makes pies for half the county. When Edmund climbs down from the cart, she hands him a list of orders as long as her arm. "Sums," she says. "Do yours again."

The twelfth morning, he doesn't come at all. No cart, no sacks, no scowl. Hattie stands in the doorway as the sky turns from black to blue to pink, a cinnamon bun cooling in her hand, and tells herself she isn't worried. She bakes with the last of the old flour. At noon she hears that a city car was seen at the mill all morning, and she has to sit down on the crooked back step.

The thirteenth morning, there is a knock at a quarter to four. Edmund is on the step, flour in his hair, a single small sack in his arms. "First grinding from the mended stones," he says. "I told the city no. My father shouted, and then he cried, and then he asked for a bun." He holds out the sack. "I thought you should bake the first loaf. Burn it, if you need to. For luck."

She doesn't burn it. She shapes it in the warm quiet with him watching from the doorway, and when it comes out of the oven, round and golden and singing as it cools, she cuts it in two and gives him half. "A baker's dozen," he says, mouth full. "Twelve mornings, and one for luck." Then he leans down, and she rises onto her toes, and he kisses her, tasting of crust and cinnamon.

These days the flour is never late. The wheel at Ashcombe Mill turns all year round, and the cart comes up the lane at four with two people on the seat instead of one. The back step has finally been mended, though Edmund complained about the job the whole time. And every morning, before the village wakes, there is a cinnamon bun waiting for him, slightly too sweet, which he eats very slowly, in the doorway, watching her.

books.title: The Night Ferry
books.author: Corin Ashdown
books.blurb: One woman saw a man fall into the black sea. The crew say every passenger is accounted for.
pages: The Marguerite left Port Ellery at eleven, an hour late, with the rain coming sideways off the harbour wall. I had a seat ticket, not a cabin, which meant a bench in the forward lounge and a paper cup of tea that tasted of the urn. I didn't mind. I had taken the night crossing to Calloway every winter for nine years, ever since my sister moved there, and I liked the hum of the engines through the floor.

A man sat down beside me just after midnight. Grey wool coat, a battered leather satchel he kept on his knees, spectacles he cleaned twice in five minutes. He offered me a peppermint from a paper twist.

"Ansel," he said, when I asked. "Ansel Crane. I don't like boats." He said it lightly, but he watched the lounge doors the whole time we talked, and he never once let go of that satchel.

At half past one I went out on the aft deck for air. The rain had thinned to a fine cold spray and the lights of the mainland were long gone. There was nothing out there but black water and the white churn of our wake.

Ansel was at the rail. Another man stood close behind him, a tall shape in a crew jacket, and for a moment I thought they were sharing a cigarette.

Then the tall man stepped back, and Ansel was not at the rail any more.

I did not scream. I have thought about that a great deal since. I simply ran to the rail and saw the grey coat turning over once in the wake, already far behind. There was a life ring in a bracket by my hand. I tore it free and threw it as hard as I could into the dark.

When I turned round, the tall man had gone. I ran for the bridge, shouting, and within ten minutes I was sitting in the purser's office with a blanket I hadn't asked for round my shoulders.

The purser was a soft-spoken man called Mr. Dunmore, with very clean fingernails. He listened, nodded, wrote nothing down, and asked me twice whether I had been drinking.

They did a count. I'll give them that. Crew went cabin to cabin and bench to bench with clipboards while the ship slowed and turned in a lazy, half-hearted circle, its searchlight wandering over the waves.

Two hundred and twelve passengers had boarded at Port Ellery. Two hundred and twelve were aboard. Mr. Dunmore showed me the list with a sympathetic smile. "Everyone is accounted for, madam. Including Mr. Crane."

"Cabin fourteen," he said. "He was asleep when the steward knocked. Perhaps you saw someone throw a bag of rubbish over, and the rain did the rest."

The life ring, he added, must have been knocked loose by the wind. The ship turned back onto its course. The searchlight went out. And I sat there with my cold tea and the absolute certainty that I was being handled.

I asked to see Mr. Crane. Mr. Dunmore sighed, but he took me down the corridor himself and knocked on fourteen.

The man who opened the door wore a grey wool coat and spectacles. He was about the right height. He had the satchel on the bunk behind him. He looked at me without a flicker of recognition and said, politely, that he was sorry for my trouble.

"Thank you for the peppermint earlier," I said. He hesitated, and smiled. "Not at all."

But I had given him one back, you see, from my own coat pocket, and Ansel had laughed and said mine were better than his. This man did not know that. He did not know my face. And the coat on his shoulders was dry as a biscuit, though Ansel had stood out in the rain for half an hour.

I said goodnight and let Mr. Dunmore walk me back to the lounge. Then I sat where I could see the corridor, and I thought.

Someone had put a stranger in Ansel's cabin, wearing a spare coat, so the count would come out even. That took planning. That took crew. And it meant the tall man in the crew jacket was still aboard, and knew exactly who had thrown that ring.

I did the only thing I could think of. In the lounge there was a radio telephone for passengers, coin-operated, meant for calling ahead to hotels. I fed it every coin I had and asked the operator for the coastguard at Calloway.

I kept my voice low. I gave the ship's name, the time, our heading, and the words life ring, grey coat, half past one. Then I hung up and waited.

Mr. Dunmore found me twenty minutes later. He sat down very close, in the seat where Ansel had been, and said the weather was dreadful for small boats. He said a woman alone might easily slip on a wet deck. He said it kindly, the way he said everything.

I told him I had already telephoned the coastguard. I watched the colour leave his clean, careful face.

We docked at Calloway at dawn. There were two police cars on the quay and a coastguard officer in a yellow coat, and none of the crew were allowed off.

The officer came straight to me. A trawler working the night lines had picked up a man an hour after I called, half frozen, clinging to a life ring with the word MARGUERITE stencilled round it in red.

He had been carrying the shipping company's ledgers, it turned out, the real ones, showing which old ferries had been sunk on purpose for the insurance. The satchel on the bunk in cabin fourteen was full of blank paper. The real one had gone over the side with him, strapped across his chest.

The tall man in the crew jacket was found in the engine room, trying very hard to look busy.

I visited Ansel in the cottage hospital that afternoon. He was pink again, and furious, and cheerful about being furious. I told him the crew had sworn nobody was missing.

"They were right, in a way," he said. "You noticed." Then he held out his hand, and in it was a sodden paper twist with one peppermint left inside. I still have the paper. I don't take the night ferry any more.

books.title: Room Nine
books.author: Marian Selkirk
books.blurb: A week at the seaside Gull Inn, where Room 9 is always one night ahead of everyone else.
pages: Monday. Arrived at the Gull Inn on the last bus, with rain on the windows and the sea throwing itself at the harbour wall. Mrs Kettle, the landlady, is small and brisk and smells of toast. She gave me Room 9, at the very top of the stairs, past a tall clock on the landing that ticks like someone tapping a pencil. The room is plain and clean and looks straight out to sea. I have come here to rest. I mean to do exactly that.

Tuesday. A strange start. There was a newspaper on my mat this morning, which was kind, except that it was dated Wednesday. At breakfast I mentioned the gale in the night, and the two retired gentlemen at the next table looked at me blankly. There had been no gale. The sky outside was blue and still. I laughed it off: a printer's error and a vivid dream. It is what I came here for, after all. Sleep deep enough to dream.

Wednesday. The gale came last night, exactly as I remembered it, rattling every window in the house except mine, which was quiet as a church. The newspaper I'd had a day early said the lifeboat would go out to a trawler called the Mary Bell. At noon the maroons went up over the harbour, and I stood on the front and watched it go. Tonight I asked Mrs Kettle, as lightly as I could, whether Room 9 was unusual.

She didn't pretend not to understand. She wiped her hands on her apron and sighed. "Nine runs a night ahead, love. Always has, since my grandmother's day. Like a clock that gains. Don't let it fret you."

Then, as I reached the stairs: "Only don't keep it too long. And come down for breakfast every morning, mind. It helps the house keep hold of you." I said I would. I don't know why I didn't ask to change rooms.

Thursday. I have been useful today, which I have not been in a long while. Tomorrow's paper on my mat said a squall would catch the small boats off the point at four. I went down to the harbour, found the fisherman whose name was printed there, Tom Brae, mending his nets, and begged him to stay in. He looked at me for a long moment. "You're in Nine," he said. Not a question. He stayed in. At four, the squall came.

Friday. When I opened my door this morning, the house wasn't there yet. The stairs were there, and the clock, but everything was grey and still: the dining room chairs upturned on the tables, no smell of toast, no sound at all. I sat on the bottom step and waited. Slowly, like a tide, it came in round me. Voices, cutlery, the kettle, Mrs Kettle in the middle of a sentence. "There you are, love," she said. "Very late down."

I asked her what happens to people who keep Nine too long. She was quiet a while. Then she told me about a Mr Lowe, years ago, a sweet old gentleman who stayed one whole winter. "He wrote us letters, after," she said. "Nice letters, thanking us for the stay. They came dated the next week, and the week after, and further. The last was dated a year on. Then they stopped." She put her hand on mine. "Go home, Miss Fenn."

Saturday. I have packed. The bus leaves at ten past eleven from the harbour, and my ticket is in my glove. But when I went to the desk to fetch my pen, there was a note there in my own handwriting, the ink still bright. It said: Don't take the bus. Nothing else. I have been sitting on the bed with my coat on for an hour, looking at it. I know my own hand. I know it was written tomorrow.

Later. I did not take the bus. I watched it go along the front from my window, small and yellow, and felt my whole chest go still, with relief or dread, I can't tell which. I went down to tell Mrs Kettle I'd stay another night. The house took much longer to arrive this time. When it came, it came thin, like a photograph left in the sun, and Mrs Kettle's voice seemed to reach me from another room.

Sunday? Or Monday. The paper on my mat is dated four days on, and I have stopped reading it. Each night I sleep, the room moves on and the house stays where it is, and the distance between us grows. I hear the waves before they break. I hear the gulls before they cry. This afternoon I heard church bells for a wedding that hasn't been arranged yet. It was lovely, actually. I hope they will be very happy.

Later still. I tried to go down. The stairs were grey and quiet all the way to the bottom, and the front door would not open, the way a door won't open in a dream. I waited on the step for hours. The house did not come. Only, very faintly, the tall clock behind me, ticking like a pencil tapped on a desk somewhere far away. I've come back up. The sea, at least, is the same sea. It is always here.

Tuesday. Last entry, I think. I am sitting at the window, and I can see, faint as steam on glass, a little woman in an apron coming up the stairs with fresh towels. She is a long way behind me now. Back on Monday, I should think. She'll knock, and I won't answer, and she'll find the bed made and the bill paid and this book on the desk. Hello, Mrs Kettle. Thank you for the toast. Don't let it fret you.

A note on the last page, in a different hand: Found this in Nine on Monday morning, with the bed made, the bill paid in full and the window open on the sea. No sign of Miss Fenn on the bus or at the harbour. The last entry above is dated Tuesday. Today is Monday. I've locked Nine and stopped the landing clock. I find I don't want to know what it says tomorrow. M. Kettle, the Gull Inn.

books.title: Letters to the Wrong Address
books.author: Imogen Ashby
books.blurb: Two strangers keep receiving each other's post, and begin, cautiously, to write back.
pages:
Dear Occupant of 3 Bramble Lane, Lower Wethering,

I enclose your dentist's reminder, your electricity bill, and a postcard from someone called Auntie Pam, who is having a marvellous time by the sea. They all came to me, at 3 Bramble Lane, Upper Wethering. Our new postman is very kind and cannot tell an Upper from a Lower. I have not read the postcard. Well. Only the front.
Yours, C. Hart

Dear C. Hart,

Thank you. I had been waiting for that bill with dread, and you returned it to me promptly, which seems unkind of you. In exchange, please find your seed catalogue, a parcel that hums faintly, and a letter marked URGENT: BEES. I hope the bees are all right. The parcel is definitely humming. I have put it on the step and backed away.
Yours, J. Pike (clocks mended, no bees)

Dear J. Pike,

The bees are fine. The humming parcel was a new queen, posted from a breeder in the north, and she is now settled and thoroughly in charge. Thank you for not opening her. Most people would have. I see from your note that you mend clocks. Mine stopped at twenty past four, and I have grown rather fond of it being twenty past four, but I suppose I ought to know the time.
Clementine Hart

Dear Clementine Hart,

Post it, if you like, and trust our postman, which I wouldn't. Twenty past four is a fine time to be stuck at. It's when the light goes gold in winter. I moved here in the autumn, after a long while in a city where every clock was telling me I was late. I'm finding I don't miss them.
J. Pike
P.S. Another of yours came this morning, from a seed company. They are very anxious about your sweet peas.

Dear Mr Pike,

The sweet peas are a professional matter. I paint the pictures on seed packets, and I grow everything I paint, to get it right. That is why my garden is a riot and my house is full of jam jars of brushes. I posted you the clock. It was delivered to the vicarage. The vicar brought it round himself, quite pink, and stayed for tea. I think the post office owes us both an apology.
Clem

Dear Clem, if I may,

Your clock is mended. It was only a hair of a spring, bent the way a hair bends when it's tired. I've put it right and polished the case, and I've left the hands at twenty past four, because I couldn't bring myself to set it to anything else. Set it yourself when you're ready. I've wrapped it in three layers and written UPPER on it in very large letters.
Jonah

Dear Jonah,

It arrived, at the right house, which I take as a sign. I sat with it on the kitchen table and listened to it tick for an hour before I wound it. My father gave it to me. It stopped the week he died, and I couldn't bear to have it mended by anyone who'd be brisk about it. You weren't brisk. Thank you. I'm sending honey. It's labelled LOWER, in capitals, twice.
Clem

Dear Clem,

The honey tastes of summer and something sharp I can't place. Lime blossom, my neighbour says, and then she asked who I was writing to, smiling in a way I didn't care for. I said a beekeeper. She said, the one in Upper? With the hat? So now I know you have a hat. I find I'm curious about the hat. I find I'm curious about a great deal, actually.
Jonah

Dear Jonah,

It is a large straw hat with a veil, and I look like a lampshade in it. Your neighbour is the postmistress's cousin, so both villages now know we write. Our postman has started delivering our letters correctly, every single time, which feels like a personal insult. Tell me something true about you. Not the clocks. Something you would only ever put in a letter.
Clem

Dear Clem,

Something true. I left the city because I'd become a man who was always in a hurry and never arrived anywhere. I sat on a train once, between two meetings, and realised I couldn't remember the last time anyone had written me a letter that wasn't a bill. Then a stranger sent back my electricity bill with a note about a postcard, and I laughed out loud on my own doorstep. That's true.
Jonah

Dear Jonah,

The summer fair is on Saturday, on the old bridge, where the two villages meet in the middle. There's a cake stall and a brass band and a man who guesses the weight of pigs. I'll be at the honey table from two o'clock. I'll be wearing the hat. If you'd like to come, come. If you'd rather we kept on writing, I'll understand, and I'll still write back.
Clem

Dear Clem,

I'll come. I've written that, and crossed it out, and written it again, and now I'm posting it before I lose my nerve. But I should warn you of something. I think we may already have met. Last October, at the market, over the last jar of damson jam, a woman in a very large hat told me I had the manners of a goose. If that was you, I apologise. You were right.
Jonah

Dear Jonah,

It was me. You had a scarf the colour of mustard, and you said damsons were wasted on people who put jam on scones. I have thought about that remark far more often than is reasonable. You were wrong, for the record. Bring a scone on Saturday and I'll prove it. And wear the scarf, so that I'll know you in the crowd.
Clem

Dear Clem,

I'm writing this at my kitchen table, which is ridiculous, since you are sitting across it, laughing at me and eating my last scone. But I wanted it on paper. You were right about the jam. You were right about the hat, too: it is a lampshade, and I love it. And when I kissed you on the bridge, the band played on and the pig was weighed, and I didn't hear a single clock.
Jonah

Dear Jonah,

I've sold the house in Upper. From next month there will be only one 3 Bramble Lane that matters, and it's in Lower, and our poor postman will have nothing left to get wrong. I'm bringing the bees, and the paints, and the clock. It tells the right time now. I set it the morning after the fair, and it hasn't stopped since.
Yours, at last at the right address,
Clem

books.title: Seven Keys
books.author: Mabel Thornquist
books.blurb: A locksmith reaches a storm-bound manor to open a safe. Nobody inside is telling the truth.
pages:
The storm had brought down two trees across the Harrowgate road, so the woman in the oilskin coat walked the last mile. She arrived at the manor a little before nine, soaked to the knee, carrying a canvas tool roll and a ring of old iron keys that clinked at her belt.

The door was opened before she knocked. "You'll be the locksmith," said the butler. "You're late."

"Vell," she said, shaking the rain from her hat. "Trees down. Couldn't be helped."

He took her coat without looking at it and led her across a hall where every lamp was lit and every portrait seemed to be leaning forward to listen. The house smelled of beeswax and cold ashes. Somewhere upstairs a shutter banged, over and over, like someone who would not stop knocking.

They were waiting in the library. Lady Ashby, the widow, in black silk and too many pearls. Her nephew Julian, young and handsome, with a signet ring he kept turning. And Dr. Fenwick, the family physician, who stood by the fire as if he had been told to stand by the fire.

"My late husband's safe," said Lady Ashby. "He took the combination with him. We need his will."

The safe was in the strongroom behind the library, through an iron door set in panelled oak. Inside, the safe itself squatted against the wall, green paint and brass dials, older than anyone in the room.

Vell knelt and unrolled her tools. She laid her ear against the cold metal and began, very slowly, to turn the first dial. Behind her, nobody spoke. But she could feel them watching each other.

She noticed things, because that was her trade. The butler had needed three tries to find the strongroom light switch. Julian's signet ring bore a crest, but the gold was bright and unscratched, bought last week. Lady Ashby's hands, folded on her silk, were rough across the knuckles, a working woman's hands.

And Dr. Fenwick's bag, by the fire, held no instruments at all. It was empty, and waiting.

At half past ten the lamps flickered and died. In the dark she heard Julian whisper to the butler, too quietly for the others: "When it opens, you take the case. Leave her with the tools in her hands. The constable will be here by midnight."

Then the lamps came back, and Lady Ashby was murmuring to the doctor, and Vell guessed she was saying much the same thing.

So that was the shape of it. Four thieves who had found a grand house empty for the season, walked in, and given themselves names. They needed a locksmith to open what they could not. And someone had telephoned the police, anonymously, to arrive just in time to find a stranger kneeling at an open safe.

Each of them, she suspected, also meant to leave with the case alone.

Vell turned the second dial, and the third. She took her time. She asked the butler for a glass of water, and noted that he went to the wrong door twice. She asked Julian what his uncle had been like, and he said, "Generous," which made her smile into the brass.

The old lord had been many things. Generous had never been one of them.

The safe had seven locks: three dials and four keyholes, set in a row like a mouth with missing teeth. "There are no keys," said Lady Ashby sharply. "We looked everywhere."

"Locksmiths carry a great many keys," said Vell, and unhooked the iron ring from her belt. She chose one without looking. It turned. So did the next, and the next, and the last, as sweetly as if it had been oiled yesterday.

The door swung open. All four of them leaned in together, and for one moment they were exactly what they were: greedy, and frightened of each other.

Inside lay a single leather case. Julian reached for it. So did the butler. Lady Ashby said, "Don't you dare," in a voice with no silk in it at all, and the doctor quietly picked up the fire iron.

Vell stepped back through the strongroom door while they were still arguing. She swung it shut. She chose the seventh key on her ring, the long black one, and locked it. The argument on the other side stopped very suddenly. Then the hammering began.

"You can't," Julian shouted through the iron. "Who do you think you are?" It was a fair question. Nobody had asked it all night.

She went into the library, sat in the good chair by the fire, and poured herself a small glass of the old lord's brandy. They had been drinking it all evening without, she noticed, the faintest idea what it was worth.

The police arrived at five to midnight, two constables in dripping capes. They had been told to expect a burglar at the safe.

"There are four of them in the strongroom," she said. "The case they wanted holds my husband's letters, and nothing else. The real will is with my solicitor in town. I'd have told them, but they never asked."

The older constable stared. Then he took off his helmet. "Lady Harrow. We understood you were abroad until spring." She smiled. "I came home early. Trees down. Couldn't be helped."

She had walked up from the station in the storm and seen strangers in her windows. She had gone round by the kitchen garden, and the man playing butler had opened the door and named her the locksmith before she could speak. So she had become one. Her father had made those locks. She had known the keys since she was six.

It had seemed rude to correct them.

The real locksmith arrived at dawn on a borrowed bicycle, soaked through, full of apologies about the trees. Lady Harrow gave him breakfast in the kitchen and paid him for his trouble. He asked whether there had been a safe to open after all.

"There was," she said, "and a strongroom to lock. I managed." She touched the iron ring at her belt. "Seven keys. You only ever need the right one."

books.title: The Scarecrow Counts
books.author: Josiah Hobb
books.blurb: Each morning the scarecrow faces a new way, and another button is missing from its coat.
pages: The scarecrow at Lowfield had stood in the barley longer than Tib Marsh had been alive. Grandad called him Old Jack. He had a sack face with a stitched smile, a hat gone green with weather, and a long brown coat with seven brass buttons down the front, which Tib had once polished for a dare. Every morning of Tib's eleven years, Old Jack had faced the lane. Then, one cold morning in late September, he didn't.

He faced the woods. Tib stood at the field gate with the milk pail and stared. The pole was the same pole, sunk deep in the same black earth. The arms were still stretched wide on their crosspiece. But the sack face had turned clean round, and now it looked away over the stubble towards the dark line of the trees. There was no wind to speak of. There hadn't been, all night.

"Someone's turned him," said Mam at breakfast, buttering toast. "Lads from the village, larking about." But the village lads were scared of Lowfield, and anyway there were no footprints in the dew. Grandad said nothing at all. He only went and stood at the kitchen window with his tea going cold, looking out at the scarecrow, and when he came back to the table he didn't finish his breakfast. Tib noticed that. He noticed most things.

On the doorstep the next morning there was a brass button. Tib knew it at once. He ran to the field, and there was Old Jack, facing north-east now, towards the old quarry, with six buttons on his coat instead of seven. The thread where the seventh had been was neat, as if it had been snipped with scissors. Tib put the button in his pocket. It was cold as a stone from a stream, and it stayed cold all day.

Another morning, another button: five left. Old Jack faced east, towards the river. The next day, four, and he faced south, towards the road. Tib began to keep a chart on the back of his school book, with the days and the buttons and an arrow for each direction. The arrows went round and round the farm like the hand of a clock. And they always pointed at the edge of something: the trees, the water, the dark.

"He's counting," Tib told Grandad, out by the woodpile. "Counting down. When the buttons are gone, something happens." Grandad split a log, and then another, before he answered.

"Happen he is," he said. "Happen it does. You leave him be, Tib. You hear me? Whatever you think of him." But Tib had already decided what he thought. The buttons in his pocket were cold, and the stitched smile was much too wide.

On the night of the third button he couldn't sleep. From his window he could see the field silver under a low moon, and Old Jack in the middle of it, facing west. And there, at the far edge of the stubble, exactly where the arrow on his chart pointed, something stood in the hedge. Something tall and thin, taller than the hedge, the colour of mist and dry stalks. Tib blinked. It was gone. Old Jack had not moved.

The next day, two buttons. Tib's mind was made up. That evening, while Mam was at the sink and Grandad dozed by the stove, he took the matches from the mantel and crept out across the field in the dusk. Old Jack loomed over him, arms wide against the last of the light. Up close, the stitched smile was not wide at all. It was only patient. Tib's hands shook as he struck the match.

A hand closed over his. Grandad's, rough as bark. He blew the match out gently. "I said leave him be," he said, not angry, only tired. Then he turned Tib round by the shoulders, the way the scarecrow faced. "Look where he's looking, lad. Not at him. Look where he's looking." Tib looked. At the edge of the trees, much closer than the hedge had been, something tall and pale was standing very still.

"It comes round once in a long while, when the harvest's in," Grandad said quietly, walking him back to the house. "Circles a farm. Looks for a way in. Takes the luck out of a place, and the warmth with it. Your gran made Jack the year it came for her father's farm. He watches it. He counts the nights it's got left to find a gap. That's all the buttons are, Tib. He's telling us how long."

"And when they're all gone?" Tib asked. Grandad opened the kitchen door on warm light and the smell of bread. "Then we stop indoors, and draw the curtains, and let him do his work."

On the last night there was one button left on Old Jack's coat. Tib went to bed when he was told. He drew his curtains, and did not open them once, though he lay awake a long time listening to a wind that wasn't there.

In the morning the field was white with frost, the first of the year. Across the stubble came a trail of long, narrow prints, set far apart, from the trees right up to the yard gate. There they stopped. They did not go round. They did not go back. And Old Jack was standing at the gate, pole and all, facing outward, his coat stiff with rime, and the last brass button lying on the step.

They carried him back to the barley together, Tib and Grandad, and set his pole in its old hole, and turned him to face the lane. That evening Mam sat by the stove and sewed all seven buttons back on, one by one, with strong brown thread. Tib held the lamp for her. When she bit off the last thread, he could have sworn the sack face looked a little less tired.

Old Jack faced the lane all that winter, and all the next year, and the year after that. Tib grew tall, and polished the buttons every spring without being dared. But he kept the chart in the back of his school book, and a reel of strong brown thread in his pocket, and he never quite stopped checking. Because Grandad had said once in a long while. And that meant there would be a next time.

books.title: A Pattern for Two
books.author: Marigold Finch
books.blurb: Eleven years of county-fair rivalry, one shared stall, and a blanket that needs both their hands.
pages: For eleven years Callum Pryce has beaten me at the Hollins County Fair by exactly one ribbon. Not every year. He is too clever for that. Some years I take the blue for colourwork and he takes it for lace, and we nod at each other across the judging tent like two cats on opposite fences. But on the years that count, he wins. I keep his red rosettes in a biscuit tin to prove it.

So when Mrs. Odell of the fair committee told me, this June, that the storm had flattened the east marquee and I would be sharing Stall Nine with Mr. Pryce, I laughed. Then I saw her clipboard and stopped.

'There's more,' she said. 'This year's Grand Showpiece is a joint entry. Two knitters, one pattern. The committee has paired you.' She said it the way you'd tell someone their cow had wandered into church.

Callum arrived at the stall on Monday with a folding chair, a flask of tea and a face like a closed gate. He is tall and long-fingered, with grey at his temples he did not have when we were twenty-five, and he knits the way some men play the violin, as if the yarn might take offence.

'Ashby,' he said, and I said, 'Pryce.' We sat with our backs to each other the entire afternoon.

The trouble is that our styles do not agree. I knit in colour: fat stripes, sheep marching round a yoke, fir trees in three greens. Callum knits in air. His shawls are so fine you could pull one through a wedding ring, all holes and patience. 'A blanket,' I said on Tuesday. 'Something people can actually use.'

'A christening shawl,' he said. 'Something people will actually remember.' His tea went cold while we argued.

On Wednesday a little girl stopped at our stall and asked if we were married, because we fought like her grandparents. Callum went the colour of my cranberry wool. I told her we were rivals, which is a sort of marriage without the cake.

After she left he was quiet a long while. Then he said, 'What if the centre is lace and the border is yours? Air in the middle. Weather round the edge.' It was, I am sorry to report, a very good idea.

We drew the pattern on the back of a feed-store calendar. He did the centre, a spray of leaves opening like a hand. I charted the border, a band of hills with tiny sheep walking all the way round, and at each corner a farmhouse with one lit window. He asked why the window.

'So whoever's under it knows someone's waiting up,' I said, and wished I hadn't, because he looked at me as though I had said something private.

We knitted in shifts. He took mornings, I took evenings, and the blanket passed between us in a basket like a sleeping baby. Somewhere in the second week I stopped finding fault with his tension. Somewhere in the third I began to read the little notes he left pinned to the work.

Row 140: your hills are crooked. I like them crooked. Row 212: brought you the good biscuits. Don't tell Mrs. Odell.

Then, on a Thursday, I found the tin. Callum had left his satchel open, and inside was a tin very like my own, and in it were labels. Fair labels. Nine years of them, each from a piece of mine sold at the craft table after judging: a hat, mittens, the fox cardigan I had been so proud of. Purchaser: anonymous. Every one of them kept, flattened and dated in his tidy hand.

I said nothing that day. I could not have, with my heart going like a loom. I went home and took out my own tin and counted his red rosettes, and for the first time I noticed I had never thrown a single one away. You do not keep eleven years of losing unless the person you lost to matters.

That evening my rows came out uneven. I left them. Crooked, apparently, was liked.

The night before judging we sat up together to finish. Rain drummed on the stall canvas, and the fairground lights made puddles of pink and gold. He worked the last leaf of the centre while I grafted the final corner, and our needles met in the middle like two people reaching for the same door handle.

'I bought your fox cardigan,' he said, not looking up, and I told him I knew. I had found the tin.

He put his knitting down. 'I wear it on Sundays,' he said. 'It's too small in the arms. I don't care.' I asked why he had never said.

'Because every year you looked at me across that tent as if you'd like to push me in the duck pond. And every year I thought, well, at least she's looking.' He laughed, a little helpless. 'Eleven years, Del. I'm a very slow knitter in some respects.'

In the morning the judges walked round our blanket twice. One of them lifted the lace to the light and the leaves threw shadows on her hand. Another counted the sheep in the border and found forty-one, though I had charted forty. Callum had knitted in an extra one, a little apart from the flock, heading for the lit window.

'That one's you,' he murmured. 'Finally coming home.'

We won, of course. A single blue rosette, which caused a small crisis, since there was only one of it and two of us. Mrs. Odell suggested we take turns. Callum suggested something else, there by the tea urn, and then he kissed me in front of half the county and a prize-winning marrow, and I found I did not mind who was watching at all.

That was three summers ago. The rosette hangs in our kitchen now, above a tin full of red ones, which we keep for sentimental reasons. We still argue over every pattern. He says colour is shouting, and I say lace is whispering in a draughty room.

He still wears the fox cardigan on Sundays. I let out the arms the first winter. It took me one evening. It had only been waiting for someone to ask.

books.title: The Quiet Witness
books.author: Ruth Pemberly
books.blurb: A deaf woman reads two strangers planning a theft across a crowded café. Nobody believes her.
pages:
Statement of Delia Marsh, given at Fairhaven police station, in writing, at her own request.

I am thirty-four years old. I have been deaf since I was two. I read lips, in English and passably in French, and I have done so every day of my life. I want that set down first, because it is the thing nobody would listen to, and it is the reason this statement exists.

On Tuesday the ninth I was at the Copper Kettle on Mill Street at about eleven in the morning, at my usual table by the radiator. It was busy. I am told it was very loud. Loud rooms make no difference to me, which is one of the few advantages I have, and I am fond of it.

Two men sat at the window table, directly across from me.

One was heavy-set, in a tweed cap, with a moustache that hid half his top lip, which was annoying. The other was thin and clean-shaven, with a scar through one eyebrow, and he spoke clearly and carefully, the way people do when they think they are being quiet.

I was not trying to read them. I want that noted too. But you cannot stop seeing what is in front of you.

The thin man said: Thursday, the Larkspur Rooms, the afternoon sale. He said: lot forty-one, the brooch. He said: when the auctioneer calls the clocks, the room gets noisy and everyone watches the clocks. He said: the case is swapped on the porter's trolley, and you walk out the side door with the crates.

The heavy man said something under the moustache. The thin man laughed, and said: Nobody looks at porters.

Then the thin man glanced round the room, and his eyes passed over me. He said, I am quite sure of it: Don't worry about her, she's deaf. I saw her signing to the waitress.

He was right that I am deaf. He was wrong about what that means. I finished my tea, which had gone cold, and wrote down everything I had read on the back of a receipt.

I went to the café owner first, Mr. Tabb, because I know him. He read my note, patted my hand, and wrote back: Probably talking about a film, love.

I then came here, to this station, and showed my note to the constable at the front desk. I will not name him. He read it slowly, and then he spoke to me, too fast and turned half away.

I asked him to face me. He did, eventually, and said very loudly, as if volume were the problem, that lip-reading was mostly guesswork, wasn't it, and that he couldn't open an inquiry because a lady had watched two strangers chatting. He said: Thank you for your concern.

I read him perfectly well. I also read him say to his colleague afterwards: Bless her. That, I could have done without.

On Wednesday I went back to the Copper Kettle at eleven. I am not proud of how much I hoped they would be there. They were.

This time the thin man sat with his back to me. I think he had noticed me noticing. But the café window behind the heavy man was dark with rain, and in the glass I could see the thin man's face, reflected, quite clearly.

Reading a reflection is reading backwards. It is hard. I had practised it as a girl on the bus, in the windows at night, for fun. He said: Ten past three, roughly. He said: The porter's name is Colley, he's paid. He said: If anything goes wrong, drop it in the umbrella stand by the side door and walk.

I wrote it all down, and that evening I made a decision.

On Thursday I went to the Larkspur Rooms for the afternoon sale. I registered as a bidder, which I have never done before, and took a seat near the side door, by the umbrella stand.

I saw them both. The heavy man was in a porter's brown coat now, with a trolley. The thin man sat in the third row with a catalogue, and nodded to people as if he belonged there.

At eleven minutes past three the auctioneer began the clocks. Everyone turned to look at a tall walnut longcase being wheeled forward. I did not. I watched the thin man's mouth.

He turned to the heavy man by the trolley and said one word: Now. I stood up, walked to the security guard at the side door, and gave her the card I had written in advance.

The card said: The porter with the moustache has just taken lot forty-one from the case on his trolley. He will try to put it in this umbrella stand. Please look in his left coat pocket. I am deaf, and I am not mistaken.

The guard was a young woman. She read the card, looked at me once, properly, and nodded. That was all it took. One person looking properly.

The heavy man came past us two minutes later with his trolley. He paused by the umbrella stand. The guard put her hand on his arm, and he went very still, and the brooch was in his left coat pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief.

The thin man was in the street by then. But I had given the guard his description too, and the constables outside were waiting.

I understand the porter, Colley, has also been spoken to. I understand the thin man is being asked about several other auction rooms. I am told the brooch is worth more than my flat.

I am setting this down because the constable who took my note on Tuesday is the one now sitting across from me, writing these pages out in fair copy. He has been facing me the whole time.

I would like one more thing recorded, please, in his handwriting. I did not overhear anything. I have never overheard anything in my life. I saw it, plainly, with my own eyes, across a crowded room, the way I see everything. Next time a woman like me brings you a note, read it as carefully as she read them.

Signed, Delia Marsh. Witnessed by the constable, who is nodding.

books.title: What the Snow Kept
books.author: Ida Marchbank
books.blurb: Every morning, fresh footprints cross the deep snow to the cabin door. None ever lead away.
pages:
Kessel Pass Weather Hut. Winter log, kept by T. Brekke, relief keeper.

Day 1. Arrived on the last supply sled before the pass closed. The driver would not stay for coffee. The hut is sound: one room, a stove, a bunk, instruments on the roof, seven coat hooks by the door. Snow already to the windowsill. The previous keeper, A. Lund, left in a hurry. His log is on the shelf.

Day 2. Wind north-east, temperature minus eighteen. Read Lund's log by the stove. Dull, mostly. Readings, firewood, a fox he named Pastor. Then his entries grow short near the end, and stop in the middle of a line. The last whole sentence reads: Another set this morning.

No idea what he meant. He did not finish his winter. Nobody at the station would tell me why.

Day 4. Fresh snow overnight, a hand's depth, smooth as paper. This morning there were footprints in it.

One set, a man's boots, coming up the slope from the tree line, straight to my door. They stop on the step. I looked all round the hut. There are no prints leading away, no prints anywhere else. Nobody knocked. I sleep lightly. I would have heard. Will watch tonight.

Day 5. Did not sleep. Sat by the window till four with the lamp out. Saw nothing. Heard nothing but the stovepipe ticking.

At first light there were two sets. The first, filled in a little by drift. And a new one beside it, narrower, a smaller boot with a worn heel, walking right up beside the other, like two people who had come together and been let in.

Day 6. Three sets. I have stopped pretending to myself.

I keep the door bolted, and the bolt is on the inside. Snow lies against the door each morning untouched, packed high, so that I have to shove it open with my shoulder. Whoever comes up the slope comes up to the step and then simply is not there. The hut feels smaller today. Warmer, too, which should be a comfort.

Day 8. When I woke, the stove was already lit. I had banked it to embers at ten. I am sure of it; I wrote it down. Now it was roaring, the kettle singing, and four tin cups set out on the table where I keep one.

I put three away. I drank from the fourth with my hands shaking. The coffee was very good. I don't know how to make it that well.

Day 9. The coat hooks. I should have written this before.

When I arrived, one hook held my coat. Since then, coats have appeared on the others. Heavy wool, waxed canvas, a red one with a fur collar. Snow melting off them, puddling on the boards, as if their owners had just come in from the slope. I counted this morning. Five coats. Five sets of prints outside.

Day 10. Went back through Lund's log with a pencil. He counted too. Day 4, one set. Day 5, two. He writes about the cups, the stove, the coats. He writes that the hut is never cold now, that he no longer feels alone, and that he is not sure he minds.

On his last day he counted seven coats. There are only seven hooks.

Day 11. Lund's coat is here. His name is stitched inside the collar in blue thread, like a schoolboy's. It hung on the sixth hook when I woke. Wet.

I do not believe he ever went down the mountain. I think he walked out one night to look at the prints, and came back up the slope like the rest of them, and the snow kept him, and the hut let him in.

Day 12. I talk aloud now, while I work, because when I stop talking I can hear the others not quite breathing. They are not unkind. Someone has darned my socks. Someone has stacked the wood more neatly than I ever do. Someone leaves the lamp turned up for me when I come in from the roof.

It would be so easy to stay, and be looked after.

Day 13. The wind has turned south and the snow has a crust on it. The pass may open in a week, but I will not wait a week. Six coats now. One empty hook beside my own.

I have packed the snowshoes, a flask, Lund's log and this one. I will go at first light, down the slope, and I will not look at the prints. I will walk away and make my own.

Day 14. Before dawn. The stove is lit again. The cups are out, seven of them, steaming. Somebody has laid my scarf by the door, folded, kind. I can feel them waiting, the way a room waits for the last guest before anyone sits down.

I am going now. If anyone finds this book: I walked down to the tree line on the fourteenth day. Look for my prints going away.

The following is written in a different hand, in pencil, below the last entry. Day 14, later. He went out at first light and we watched him from the window. He walked well, down toward the trees. The snow was kind to him for a long while.

Then the snow did what it does. By noon there was a new set coming up the slope. Long strides. Snowshoes.

His coat is on the seventh hook. He takes his coffee black. He still talks while he works, which we like, and he still says he will go down when the pass opens, which we also like.

There is a new hook by the door this morning. Nobody put it up. It is waiting. The relief keeper arrives in spring. We will have the stove lit for her.

books.title: The Keeper's Garden
books.author: Morwenna Pell
books.blurb: A botanist comes to catalogue a rare flower and finds a lighthouse keeper's impossible garden, and a reason to stay.
pages:
Gannet Rock, 3rd May. Dear Bea,

I am here, and alive, and only slightly seasick. The supply boat left me on the landing steps with two crates, a plant press and a lighthouse keeper who said nine words to me in an hour, four of them 'mind the weed, it's slippery.' The rock is a fist of granite a mile out from anywhere. There is no tree on it. There is barely a blade of grass. And yet.

And yet, Bea, behind the keeper's cottage there is a garden. I don't mean a few pots of thyme. I mean roses, a fig against the south wall, beans climbing the old signal mast, and a row of something blue I could not name, which for a botanist is an insult. The wind should have stripped it to the bone years ago. Mr. Rennick saw me staring, said 'Supper's at six,' and went up to his lamp.

6th May. Bea, he is impossible. I asked how the fig survives the winter and he said, 'Stubbornness.' I asked about the blue flowers and he said, 'Ask them.' He is perhaps fifty, broad and salt-weathered, with a wedding ring he turns with his thumb when he thinks no one is looking. The supply man told me his wife died four winters ago. I have stopped asking about the garden at supper. I ask about the weather instead, which he likes.

10th May. I have begun to understand the walls. They are not random. Someone built them in a careful spiral of dry stone, each course leaning a little inward, so the wind runs round the outside and the middle stays still as a held breath. The soil is seaweed and ash and years of patience. Whoever built this was a better gardener than I will ever be. I said so, and for the first time Mr. Rennick almost smiled.

'Anwen built it,' he told me that evening, over fish and potatoes. 'My wife. Took her eleven years. She said a lighthouse saves ships, and a garden saves the people who keep the lighthouse.' He turned his ring. 'The seeds came from sailors. Every boat that called, she'd ask what grew where they came from. Some brought packets. Some brought a pip from their dinner.'

So the blue flowers have no name because they came from somebody's pocket.

15th May. I was sent here, as you know, to find the Gannet campion, the little pink flower the old survey swore grew only on this rock. I have found it. It grows in the cracks below the lamp gallery, exactly where the light sweeps over it. Tobias, who has said I may call him Tobias, tells me it opens at night. I did not believe him. Tonight I am going to sit up and see.

16th May. It opens at night. Bea, I sat on the gallery steps in two jumpers and his old oilskin, and every time the beam came round, the campion turned its face toward it like a cat to a fire. Petals the colour of the inside of a shell. Tobias brought tea in a tin mug and sat beside me, and we watched it for an hour without a word. It was the best hour of my working life.

20th May. A storm came in on Tuesday and did not leave till Friday. We worked through it together, tying the beans, wedging sacking round the roses, carrying the potted lemons up to the lamp room, where they sat beside the great lens like passengers. At the worst of it a pane blew in at the cottage, and he stood in the gap holding a board while I hammered. We were both soaked. We both laughed. I can't remember why.

When it was over, Bea, half the garden was flattened. Tobias stood in the middle of it and I thought he might break. Instead he knelt and began lifting the beans, one by one, and said, 'She'd have been out here before the rain stopped.' So I knelt too. We rebuilt the north wall by lamplight. My hands are cut to ribbons. I have never felt so useful in my life.

28th May. The boat comes for me on the first. My work is done: the campion is drawn, pressed, measured and named in my notebook. I ought to be glad. Instead I find myself memorising things that are not science. The way he hums to the fig. The way he leaves the last of the honey for me. The way he looked at me across the wall we built, as though he had remembered something he had decided to forget.

31st May. I told him tonight that I was leaving tomorrow. He was quiet for so long I thought he hadn't heard. Then he took me to the far corner of the garden, under the spiral wall, and showed me a bed I had never noticed. Bare soil, freshly dug. 'Anwen always said the garden would want a new hand one day,' he said. 'I didn't believe her. I've dug this for whatever you'd like to plant.'

Bea, I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing useful at all. I said, 'Campion won't grow in a bed.' He said, 'Then plant something that will.' And when the lamp came round again, its light passing over us both, he kissed me, very carefully, as if I were a seedling he did not want to bruise. I am writing this by candle at two in the morning. The boat comes at ten.

1st June, the mainland. Dear Bea,

I took the boat. I owe the university my report, and I am a woman who finishes her work. But I have resigned my post from the end of summer, handed the department my notebooks, and spent my last week's wages on seeds. Two hundred packets. Sweet peas. Lavender. Something blue from a market stall whose seller couldn't name it. I think that's only proper.

Gannet Rock, 2nd September. Dear Miss Hale,

Your sister asks me to tell you she has arrived safely and cannot write this week, because her hands are in the soil. The new bed is planted. The fig has two ripe fruits and she has eaten both. The campion opened again last night and we sat up to watch it. You would be welcome to visit. Mind the weed on the steps. It's slippery. Yours, T. Rennick

books.title: Last Train to Halden
books.author: J. M. Thorne
books.blurb: Snowbound forty miles from Halden, a conductor must find a stolen ledger before the thief's friends arrive.
pages: I have been a conductor on the northern line for twenty-six years, and I can tell you a train has a sound when it is about to stop for good. A long sigh under the floor. The lamps dim and brighten. On the ninth of December, forty miles short of Halden, the Night Mail sighed, lurched, and sat down in the snow like a tired horse. Drifts ahead, the driver sent back. The plough was coming. Nobody was to leave the carriages.

First class held five passengers that night, and one locked case. The case belonged to Mr. Sorel, a thin, nervous accountant who had boarded at the coast with it chained to his wrist. He tipped me well and asked me, twice, to see that nobody disturbed him. I knew what was in it, because the whole country was talking about it. The Varga Shipping ledger. The real books, the ones that showed where a great many people's savings had gone.

The other four I can tell you quickly, because I watched them all night. Mrs. Linnet, a widow in grey, whose husband had put everything into Varga and lost it. Madame Corvin, a singer who laughed too loudly and drank only water. Felix Dane, a young clerk from the Varga offices, who kept rubbing his ink-stained fingers. And Colonel Ashgrove, white-moustached, who had taken a sleeping draught and was not to be woken for anything short of a war.

And there was a sixth, who was not supposed to be in first class at all. A big, quiet man in a second-class coat, who kept walking up the corridor and back, looking at the compartment doors. I knew his face from the newspapers. Hollis Crane, director of Varga Shipping, the man that ledger would ruin. He saw me recognise him, and he smiled, and touched his hat, and went back the way he had come.

At two in the morning Mr. Sorel cried out. I ran down the corridor with my lamp and found him on his knees in his compartment. The chain still hung from his wrist. The case lay open on the seat, empty. He had dozed, he said, only a minute; the heating made him drowsy. When he woke, the ledger was gone.

Snow was banked to the windows on both sides. Nobody could have left the train. Whoever had it was still aboard.

By half past two I had every first-class passenger in the dining car, and Mr. Crane too, who came without being asked. Everyone looked at him. He looked back, quite calm. 'Search me,' he said, spreading his hands. 'Search my compartment. You'll find nothing. I'd be a fool to take it, with half the train watching me.'

I searched him. He was right. I found nothing at all. That was the first thing that bothered me.

I searched them all, with the guard as witness, and their luggage too. Mrs. Linnet's carpet bag held her husband's letters, read so often they had gone soft as cloth. Madame Corvin's trunk held gowns and a stage pistol that could not fire. Felix Dane had a notebook full of figures copied from the ledger itself, he admitted, white-faced; he was the one who had told Mr. Sorel where to find it. No ledger anywhere.

That left the colonel, who had to be woken. He came out blinking in his dressing gown, furious. He had slept like the dead, he said; the draught saw to that. Had I no respect for an old soldier? He had served thirty years with the Northmoor Rifles, at the barracks in Callan.

I apologised and searched his compartment. Nothing. But as I left, I noticed his boots standing by the hot pipes, and under them, a small, spreading puddle.

Boots do not puddle unless there is snow on them. And a man asleep since ten does not have snow on his boots at two.

There was another thing. My father had served at Callan, and the barracks there closed the year I was born. Thirty years with the Northmoor Rifles, the colonel had said. A good, round, soldierly number. Too round. I began to think the colonel had never been a colonel, and had never been asleep.

I said nothing. I went to the end of the carriage, to the door of the vestibule, and held my lamp to the step. Snow had blown in and settled there, and pressed into it was the edge of a boot heel. The outer door had been opened and pulled shut again, and beyond it the snow was broken by a line of holes, already softening, leading away from the train toward the telegraph poles.

I put on my greatcoat and stepped down into snow to my knees. The wind took my breath. I followed the holes, one, two, a hundred, and they led to the third telegraph pole and stopped. At its foot the snow had been dug and patted flat. I knelt and dug with my hands until they ached, and my fingers struck oilcloth. Inside, dry and fat with figures, was the Varga ledger.

'I'll take that, conductor.' The colonel stood behind me, a coat over his dressing gown, and he was not blinking now. 'Mr. Crane has friends in the village yonder. They'll be along with a sledge before the plough. Hand it here, go back to your warm train, and remember nothing.'

He stepped closer. I held the lamp up between us. I am not a brave man. But I had found it, and I was not going to give it up.

Then a second light came bobbing along the line, and a voice called my name. Mrs. Linnet, in her grey coat, with the guard behind her and Felix Dane behind him, all floundering through the drifts. She had seen me go out, she told me later, and seen the colonel follow, and decided she had lost quite enough to Varga Shipping already.

The colonel looked at four lamps and one ledger, and put his hands in his pockets.

The plough reached us at dawn, throwing up white wings of snow, and behind it came no sledge at all. Perhaps Mr. Crane's friends saw the lamps along the line and thought better of it. Mr. Crane himself said nothing the rest of the journey. He sat very straight in the dining car between the guard and myself, the colonel opposite, and watched the snow go by, and he did not smile once.

At Halden the police were waiting on the platform. Mr. Sorel carried the ledger off the train himself, chained to his wrist again, and Felix Dane walked beside him like a bodyguard. Madame Corvin kissed me on both cheeks. Mrs. Linnet only shook my hand and said, 'Thank you. He'd have liked you.'

I have worked the northern line eleven more winters since. Whenever it snows, I check the boots.

books.title: The Mirewood Ferryman
books.author: Silas Fenn
books.blurb: At dusk the ferryman poles travellers across the mire, and always counts one more than he took.
pages:
Mind the step, now. The punt rocks, but she won't tip, not for you. Sit there on the middle board, where the lantern can see you. That's it.

You'll have heard of me, I expect, if you came this far into the Mirewood at dusk. The ferryman. The only way across the mire that doesn't end with your boots full of black water and the reeds closing over your head.

Push off, then. Hear that? That's the pole finding the bottom, eight feet down, soft as cake. Forty years I've poled this mire, and my father before me, and his before him. The channels move. The pools move. Only the ferryman knows where they've gone in the night.

You're quiet. That's all right. Most of my passengers are quiet, crossing over. The mist does that to folk.

Tonight I took four aboard at the willow landing, same as most nights. A pedlar with a pack of tin pans. Two sisters going home from market, sharing an apple. A young man in a good coat who paid double to sit near the front.

And you. Though I don't rightly remember you paying. No matter. I don't recall half of what I ought to, these days.

I'll tell you a thing my father told me, since we've a long way to go and the herons are settling. He said: never count your passengers on the water, boy. Count them on the landing, take their coins, and then keep your eyes on the channel.

I asked him why. He said: because the mire likes company, and it's always got some to spare.

The first time I counted on the water, I was nineteen. Took on three at the willow landing. Out past the drowned oak, I turned round with the lantern and counted four. A woman in a grey shawl, at the back, with her hands in her lap. Wet to the shoulders.

She didn't say anything. When we reached the far bank, three got off, and she was gone.

Since then I've counted every night. I can't help it. One more than I took on, every crossing, without fail. Sometimes an old man with weed in his beard. Sometimes a girl in a straw hat, years out of fashion. Never the same one twice.

They never speak. They never pay. They sit still and patient as stones, and they look at the far bank like it's home.

Mind your hand off the side. The water's colder than it looks, and there are things in it that remember being warm.

I used to be frightened of them. Now I think they're only travellers who tried to cross alone, on foot, in the mist, a long time ago, and never got to the other side. So I take them. Every dusk, one at a time. It seems only decent.

There's the drowned oak, look, with the lantern moss on it. Halfway now. I'll count, if you don't mind. Old habit. The pedlar, with his pans clinking. One. The two sisters, still on that apple. Two, three. The young man in the good coat at the front, pretending not to be afraid of the dark. Four.

And you. Five.

Don't look at me like that. I'm not accusing you of anything.

Only, would you look down at your hands for me? Go on. There's no coin in them. There never was. And your sleeves are wet to the shoulder, though it's not rained all day. And the pedlar hasn't once looked your way, though you're sitting close enough to touch his pack.

It's all right. Truly it is. They're always surprised. It's a kindness, I think, that the mire lets them forget.

You came to the edge of the Mirewood one evening, a long while back, with somewhere to be and no coin for the ferry. You thought you knew the path. The mist came down. You remember now, don't you? The reeds, and the cold, and how quiet it all went.

Hush. Don't cry. There's nothing to be done about it, and nothing more to be afraid of either. The worst of it was over long ago.

What's left is only the crossing. That's what I'm for. I can't bring anyone back, but I can bring them over. The far bank's just ahead, see, where the lights are. Somebody's lit a lamp for you.

Now, listen close, because this is the part that matters. When the punt touches the bank, the others will step off, and so will you. Walk straight up the path toward the lights. Don't wait for me. Don't turn round to see the water.

The ones who look back end up on my punt again some other dusk. The mire keeps hold of anyone who's still looking for it.

There. Feel that bump? That's the landing. Off you go, pedlar. Mind your pans. Off you go, ladies. Young sir, give me your hand, the plank's slippery.

And you. Up you get. That's it. Straight up the path. Don't look back. Don't look back. I'll be here tomorrow at dusk, the same as always, with my lantern and my pole and my counting.

Five stepped off tonight. I counted them up the path, every one, and not one turned round. The lamp at the top swung once, as if somebody had come out to meet them.

I push off empty. Or nearly. The mist is thick tonight, it's a long way back to the willow landing, and I've stopped turning round to count on the return. It's kinder not to know who sits behind me.

books.title: Second Harvest
books.author: Clementine Vale
books.blurb: Twenty-two years, forty-one lost letters, and one last apple harvest before the orchard is sold.
pages: The sign at the end of the lane said CALLOWAY ORCHARD, EST. 1911, and beneath it, newer and tied on with wire, a second sign said FOR SALE. June Calloway had hung it herself in August, on a morning so hot the wire burned her fingers. Now it was October and the trees were bowed with fruit, and the buyer's papers sat on her kitchen table under a jar of honey, waiting to be signed after the harvest.

One last harvest, she had promised herself. One last time done properly, the way her father did it: every tree picked by hand, the windfalls pressed for cider, the best russets wrapped in paper for winter. But the old pickers had grown old or moved away, and her advertisement brought exactly one reply. She knew the handwriting before she opened it. She had kept twelve letters in that hand, in a shoebox, for twenty-two years.

Theo Marsh got out of a dusty van at seven on Monday morning, and June's first thought was that he had got broad, and her second was that he had kept his terrible hat. He had left the valley at nineteen to learn cider-making somewhere far off with mountains, and promised to write every week, and he had, for twelve weeks. Then nothing.

'I heard you needed hands,' he said, and she told him she needed pickers, and the ladder was in the barn.

They worked the first rows in silence. He was quick and careful, twisting each apple off with his thumb the way her father had taught them both as children, never pulling, never bruising. By noon they had filled forty crates. By two she had stopped pretending not to watch him. At four he came down his ladder, wiped his hands, and said, 'Your letters stopped, June. Not mine.'

She nearly dropped the bushel she was carrying.

They sat on the tailgate of his van and worked it out like a sum. His thirteenth letter, and his fourteenth, and all the ones after, had come to the farm. Her father had collected the post in those years. Her father, who had wanted her to stay, who had been frightened of an empty orchard and a daughter across an ocean.

'He never said,' June whispered. 'Not once. Not even at the end.'

She did not sleep that night. At two in the morning she went through her father's desk, drawer by drawer, the task she had been avoiding since spring. At the very back, behind the seed catalogues and tax papers, she found a wooden seed box tied with baling twine. Inside were forty-one letters, unopened, all in Theo's hand. On top lay a note in her father's: I was wrong to keep these. I didn't know how to give them back.

She read them all before dawn, sitting on the kitchen floor. They were full of mountains, and apples she had never tasted, and a boy who was lonely and stubborn and kept writing to someone who never answered. The last one, from a year and a half after he left, said: I won't write again, because I think you've made your choice. But if you ever need me, I'll come. I'll always come.

And he had.

She said nothing about the letters on Tuesday. She was not ready. They picked the long row by the creek and talked, carefully, the way you step onto a frozen pond. He had a cidery now, small and good, far up a valley in the north. He had won a prize or two. He had never married. She had not either. Neither of them said why, and both of them knew.

On Wednesday he stood a long time by the oldest tree in the orchard, a gnarled russet her great-grandfather had grown from a pip he found in his coat pocket. Their initials were still in its bark, stretched wide by twenty years of growing. 'Nobody else has this apple,' Theo said. 'It's in no catalogue. If the buyer clears the orchard for houses, it's gone. From the whole world, June.'

'I know,' she said. 'Why do you think I can't sleep?'

When he told her not to sell, she shook her head. 'I can't keep it. Dad left debts. The roof leaks. The press is older than both of us.' She heard her voice crack and hated it. 'I'm not too proud to say I'm tired, Theo. I'm only too proud to be rescued.'

He nodded slowly, as if she had handed him a puzzle he meant to solve properly. 'All right,' he said. 'No rescue. Noted.'

He did not mention it again until Saturday, the last day of harvest, when the final crate was loaded and the press was groaning through the windfalls. Then he took a folded paper from his jacket. It was not a cheque. It was a plan, drawn on the back of a cider label: a second press, a little shop in the old barn, the russet grafted onto a hundred new trees, and at the bottom two names, side by side. Partners.

'I'll put in the press and the know-how,' he said. 'You put in the orchard and the bossing about. We split the work. We split the roof. And if you'd rather sell, I'll help you pack, and I'll still be glad I came.' He took a breath. 'But I think we'd make a very good cider, June. I think we always would have.'

She went inside without a word. He thought he had lost.

She came back out with two things. One was the buyer's contract, which she tore in half and in half again, and dropped into the press hopper with the windfalls. The other was a ribbon-tied bundle of forty-one letters. 'I found them,' she said. 'I've read every one. I'm sorry I'm so late writing back.'

Theo looked at the letters a long time. Then he looked at her, and took off his terrible hat.

He kissed her under the old russet, with the press thumping behind them and the last light going gold through the leaves, and it was not like being nineteen. It was better. It was like coming in from the cold to a kitchen where someone has kept the fire going.

In spring they grafted a hundred young russets. The new sign at the end of the lane says CALLOWAY AND MARSH. Nobody has taken it down.

books.title: The Crossword Setter
books.author: E. V. Quill
books.blurb: A retired crossword setter finds her own name hidden in the local paper's puzzle, and a warning beneath it.
pages: Monday 3rd March. Forty-one years I set the crossword for the Brackwater Courier under the name Magpie, and in retirement I swore never to solve anyone else's.
