It is like a chef eating in a cafe; one only suffers. But the new setter, Kestrel, has been rather good, and this morning the rain kept me in, so I did Saturday's over my toast. Eleven minutes. Then I noticed the first letters of the across answers.

Read down, the first letters of the across answers spelled WINIFRED POLE.

That is my name. It is not a common name. I sat with my toast going cold and told myself it was coincidence, that a grid has only so many letters and a vain old woman will see herself anywhere. Then I fetched the two previous Saturdays from the recycling. Their first letters spelled LIVES ALONE and BLUE DOOR. My door is blue.

Tuesday 4th March. I did not sleep well. I checked the locks twice and the back window three times, and at two in the morning I caught myself standing in the hall in my nightgown, holding the poker, listening to the fridge. This will not do. I am seventy-six, not a heroine in a paperback. In daylight I telephoned the Courier and asked who Kestrel was. The girl on the desk said the setter's name was confidential. I said I used to be confidential myself. She was unmoved.

Saturday 8th March. The new puzzle came. I did it standing on the doormat with my coat still on. The first letters across: KEY UNDER HARE.

There is a stone hare by my back step, and yes, the spare key is under it, and no, I have never told a soul. Except, I realised with a horrible cold feeling, that I had told one person. Last month, when I had the flu, I asked my new neighbour to let himself in and feed the cat.

His name is Desmond Fairley. He moved into number nine in January, a soft-spoken man with good shoes, and he has been very kind. He carries my shopping. He mended the gate. He has asked, twice, very gently, about Arthur's stamp collection, which the valuer said was worth more than this house. I told him it was in the bank. It is in the wardrobe. I do not know why I lied to him. I am very glad now that I did.

Sunday 9th March. I have gone back through every Kestrel puzzle since January, with a pencil and a pot of strong tea, and found more. Not only first letters. Diagonals, hidden words, an answer of HARE where the grid did not need one. Together they read: WINIFRED POLE. LIVES ALONE. BLUE DOOR. KEY UNDER HARE. STAMPS. TUESDAY. And this week, hidden in the down clues, a word I had missed the first time. DONT.

Don't what? Don't open the door? Don't trust him? I have set ten thousand clues in my life, and I know the difference between a threat and a warning. A threat does not trouble to hide itself in the down clues of a small-town newspaper. Somebody is planning something for Tuesday, and somebody else, Kestrel, is trying to tell me. Only me. Because who else in Brackwater would ever notice?

Monday 10th March. I went to the police. The young constable was polite and wrote everything down, and asked whether I had perhaps been doing a great many crosswords lately. I showed him the grids. He looked at them the way the cat looks at the radio. 'Any word can be found if you look hard enough, madam.' I wanted to tell him that is precisely what a setter is paid not to allow. Instead I thanked him, went home, and made a plan.

If Kestrel can hide a message in a puzzle, so can Magpie. I telephoned my old editor, Harold, who is ninety and still terrifying, and he rang the Courier, and the Courier, it turns out, is still a little afraid of him. A special Magpie puzzle, one week only, a retired setter's farewell, to run in Monday's evening edition. I set it in a single afternoon. I have not worked so fast since 1983.

My puzzle had a theme, as the best ones do: birds. Rook, finch, heron, plover. Anyone would think it sweet. But the first letters of the across answers said, to one reader only, KESTREL RING ME, and my telephone number was folded into the clue numbers. Then I sat by the telephone all evening like a girl waiting to be asked to a dance.

At six minutes past nine that night, it rang.

Her name was Tamsin. She was young and frightened, and she apologised four times before she said anything useful. Desmond Fairley was her uncle. He had done this before, in other towns, to other old people living alone: kind for a while, then one day the house is emptied and so is his. She had tried to stop him, and he laughed. She dared not go to the police herself.

'But you,' she said. 'I grew up on your puzzles. I knew you'd see.'

Tuesday 11th March. This afternoon at three, Desmond Fairley let himself in at my back door with the key from under the hare. He thought I was at the library; I had told him so, quite loudly, over the fence. He went straight upstairs to the wardrobe.

I was sitting on the landing in Arthur's armchair, with the cat on my lap and the poker across my knees, and in the bathroom behind me, door ajar, were the constable and his sergeant.

I will not pretend I was calm. My heart was going like a typewriter. But I had rehearsed my line all morning, and I said it well. 'Good afternoon, Mr. Fairley. Five letters: one who takes what is not his while the owner is out.'

He stared at me. Then the sergeant stepped out of the bathroom, and Mr. Fairley's good shoes went very quietly down my stairs between two policemen. He did not say a word. Neither, for once, did I.

Saturday 15th March. The young constable came round with flowers and an apology, and asked, rather shyly, whether I might show him how a cryptic clue works. I have given him a beginner's grid. He has got three answers and is very proud.

The Courier's crossword this week is by Kestrel, as usual. It is a good one. I did it in nine minutes. The first letters of the across answers say THANK YOU MAGPIE.

Saturday 22nd March. Tamsin came to tea today. She brought a cake, burnt on one side, and a folder of puzzles she has been setting since she was twelve. Some are clumsy. Some are very fine indeed. We sat at my kitchen table till the light went, and I showed her how to hide a word so that only the right reader finds it.

I have moved the spare key. I have told no one where. Not even you, diary.

books.title: Sixty Years Overdue
books.author: Hollis Venn
books.blurb: A moth guide comes back sixty years late, and someone keeps writing to the librarian in its margins.
pages: The book came back on a Tuesday, through the brass return slot of the Fernhollow Library, sometime between closing and dawn. Agnes Marrow found it on the mat with the morning post: a slim green volume, A Field Guide to the Lesser Moths, its cloth cover soft as felt. The date card in the back pocket bore one faded stamp. Due back the fourteenth of October, 1964. Sixty years overdue, almost to the day.

Agnes had been the librarian for eleven years, and the only one for six, since the council cut the hours. She knew every squeak of the floorboards and every reader by their borrowing. Nobody in Fernhollow was old enough to have taken this out. She turned to the borrower's line and found the name smudged away, as though a thumb had rubbed it out on purpose.

She set the book aside to process later. That was her first mistake.

At lunch she opened it to check for damage. The pages smelled of cedar and rain. The illustrations were lovely, moths drawn in soft brown ink: the Lilac Beauty, the Mottled Umber, the Old Lady with her wings folded like a shawl. And in the margin beside the Old Lady, in faint grey pencil, someone had written: Agnes, you've let the kettle boil dry again.

In the back room, the kettle was screaming.

She told herself it was a coincidence, and that Agnes was not such an unusual name. She told herself this while pulling the kettle off the ring with a tea towel, and again while she sat very still at the issue desk with the book closed in front of her.

By closing time she had almost believed it. Then she opened the book to put it in the repair tray, and found a new note on the flyleaf.

It had not been there at lunch. She was sure of that, the way you are sure of your own front door. Agnes, love. Don't shelve me with the others. I'm not finished.

The handwriting leaned to the right, looping and careful, the hand of someone taught from copybooks. She knew it. She had seen it on the backs of photographs in a biscuit tin at her mother's house, under captions like Seaside, 1958 and Me with the new bicycle.

Her grandmother, Ada Marrow, had been the librarian at Fernhollow long before her. Agnes had never met her. Ada had locked up one October evening in 1964 and walked out into a mist so thick the buses stopped running, and she had never come home. They dragged the pond and searched the beechwoods. All they found was her cardigan, folded neatly on a stile, with a single pale moth asleep on its sleeve.

Agnes did not sleep that night. She sat at her kitchen table with the field guide and a pencil of her own, and at a quarter past two, feeling foolish, she wrote in the margin: Who are you? She closed the book. She counted to a hundred. She opened it.

Beneath her question, in the leaning hand: You know who, love. I took myself out of the library that night, and I've been reading ever since.

Over the following week the notes came every evening, always on a fresh page, always a little further into the book. Ada wrote about the moths. She wrote that the drawings were doors if you looked at them long enough, and that behind them lay a quiet grey country of dusk, where it was always just before the lamps were lit.

It's beautiful here, she wrote. But it goes on and on, and I'm so tired of the evening.

Agnes began to notice moths in the library. One on the lampshade in Local History. Two on the window of the children's corner. A dozen, pale as ash, sleeping in the gaps between the encyclopaedias. They never stirred when she came close. They only seemed to be waiting. The notes changed, too. The looping hand grew shakier, and the words fewer.

Agnes. Don't read the last page. Whatever you do. That's how it keeps you.

Naturally, she wanted to. That was the cruelty of it. The last page was right there under her thumb, and she could feel the faint pull of it, the way you feel a draught from a door left open somewhere in the house. Sixty years ago her grandmother had read it, alone at this same desk, on a misty night when the buses stopped.

Agnes locked the book in the safe instead, and turned the dial, and walked home in the dark.

The note waiting the next morning was the shortest yet. It was written across the drawing of the Old Lady moth, so lightly that she had to tilt the page to the window to read it. I can't find my way back by myself. Open a window at dusk, love, and hold me open to the sky. Then let go.

Agnes looked at the calendar on the wall behind the desk. It was the fourteenth of October.

At closing time Agnes switched off every light in the library but the one over the issue desk. She opened the tall window in Local History, the one that always stuck, and the evening came in cool and smelling of leaf mould. Mist was rising from the beechwoods, white and slow, exactly as the old newspapers had described it.

She stood at the window with the field guide open across her palms, the Old Lady moth face up, and she waited.

They came from everywhere: from the encyclopaedias and the lampshades and the gaps behind the radiators, hundreds of pale moths rising soft as breath. They poured past her face and out into the mist. And among them, for the space of one heartbeat, Agnes saw the shape of a small woman in a cardigan, turning back at a stile to wave.

Then the window was only a window, and the book was very light in her hands.

She looked at the flyleaf one last time. A final note was there, the pencil firm again, the loops as neat as a schoolgirl's. Thank you, Agnes. Mark me returned. All my love, A.

Agnes stamped the date card in fresh red ink, Returned, and cried a little, and closed the window. Then she made herself a cup of tea, and for once she did not let the kettle boil dry.

The next morning there was another book on the mat beneath the brass slot. Navy cloth, gold lettering, a title she had never seen in any catalogue: A Field Guide to the Greater Dark. The date card in the back pocket bore one crisp stamp. Due back the fourteenth of October, 2084.

The borrower's name was written in a neat, upright hand that Agnes knew better than any other. It was her own.

books.title: Snowed In at the Bookshop
books.author: Rosalind Thackery
books.blurb: A blizzard, a secondhand bookshop, two strangers and the books that changed them.
pages:
The snow began at four, polite and pretty, and by six it had buried the high street up to the letterboxes. Hazel Quill, who minded the Crooked Shelf secondhand bookshop three evenings a week, watched the last bus give up at the corner and turn back towards the depot. The owner was away at his daughter's. The radio said the roads were closed until morning.

That was when she noticed she was not alone.

He was sitting on the floor of the Travel section, between the far north and the far south, with his scarf still on and snow melting off his boots. He looked up guiltily, like someone caught reading in a library after hours, which was more or less what he was.

I'm so sorry, he said. I came in for a book for my sister and lost track of time. And then I lost track of the street.

His name was Theo. He had driven up from the coast to deliver his sister's birthday present in person, and had parked his car, as far as he could tell, under a drift outside the bakery. Hazel made two mugs of tea on the little ring in the back room, found the spare blanket the owner kept for his dog, and lit the old paraffin stove, which smelled like every winter of her childhood.

They sat by the stove with the shop lamps turned low. Snow ticked against the windows. The shelves rose round them into the dark, thousands of books with their spines turned inward, listening. What book did you come for? Hazel asked.

Theo hesitated. I don't know the title, he said. That's the trouble. It's one we had as children. My sister says it changed her life. She was six.

Hazel laughed, and then said that wasn't silly at all, that most of the books that changed her had found her when she was far too young to know better. Theo asked her which ones. She said she'd tell him if he went first.

So he told her about a battered paperback called The Long Ridge, found in a guesthouse on a wet holiday when he was nineteen and sure he would be an accountant forever.

It was a memoir by a woman who had walked every mountain ridge in the north alone, with a tent and a tin mug and terrible knees. He read it in two nights. On the third morning he walked up the nearest hill in borrowed boots, in the rain, and at the top the cloud tore open and he could see the whole valley shining.

He had been a mountain guide ever since. Eleven years.

Your turn, he said.

Hazel went to the children's shelves and came back empty-handed, and sat down again, and admitted she didn't own it any more. It had been a picture book called The Fox Who Knitted for the Moon. A little fox notices the moon looks cold up there all alone, and knits her a scarf, row by row, all through the winter, out of anything she can find.

Her grandmother had read it to her every night the winter her parents split up. Afterwards her grandmother taught her to knit, with two pencils and a ball of string at first, and Hazel had never really stopped. Socks for the postman. Hats for the whole street. A scarf for the owner's dog.

It taught me you can mend a cold thing slowly, she said. One row at a time. Isn't that silly?

Theo was looking at her very strangely. A fox, he said. In a red scarf. Knitting with twigs. She unravels a bird's nest for wool, and then feels guilty and knits the birds a new one. Hazel stared at him. That's it, she said. That's the one. How do you know?

Because that's my sister's book, he said. That's the one I came for. I've been looking for it for three months.

They searched the whole shop for it by torchlight, laughing, calling titles to each other across the aisles. It was past midnight when they gave up, dusty and triumphant about nothing, and sat back down by the stove. It doesn't matter, Theo said. I'll find a copy somewhere. Honestly, I think I'm just glad to know it changed someone else too.

Hazel found that she was glad as well, unreasonably so.

They talked until the stove burned low. About the other books: the cookery book that taught Theo's father to bake bread the year his mother left; the atlas of islands Hazel had drawn routes across in felt-tip, planning journeys she still hadn't taken; the poetry anthology they had both, it turned out, failed an exam on. Outside, the snow went on falling softly, as if it had all night and nowhere else to be.

Somewhere around three, Hazel fell asleep against the poetry shelves. She woke to grey light and the scrape of a snowplough in the street, and found the spare blanket tucked round her shoulders and Theo gone.

On the counter was a note in square, careful capitals. GONE TO DIG OUT THE CAR. THANK YOU FOR THE BEST NIGHT I'VE HAD IN YEARS. Beside it lay a coin, for the tea.

She told herself she wasn't disappointed. She swept the snow off the step and turned the sign to Open, and very firmly did not look down the street towards the bakery. She had known him for one night. People who walked mountain ridges for a living did not come back to small shops in small towns.

At ten past nine the bell over the door rang, and he came back in with two coffees and a paper bag.

The car's under about four feet of snow, he said. It'll be hours. And I realised I'd left without telling you something.

He set the bag on the counter. Inside was a ball of red wool from the craft shop next to the bakery, and a book he'd found in their bargain bin: a children's picture book, a little worn at the corners, with a fox in a scarf on the cover.

It's for my sister, he said, going a bit pink. But I wondered if you'd write in it first. Something about the fox. And then I wondered if I could come back next week and tell you what she said. And the week after that, for no reason at all.

Hazel looked at the fox, and at the wool, and at him, standing in the snowlight with the coffee going cold in his hands.

She took the pen from the counter and wrote on the flyleaf: For whoever finds this. Some cold things can be mended slowly, one row at a time. Then she came round the counter and kissed him, softly, while the snowplough went by and the bell over the door was still swinging.

He came back the next week, and the week after that, and he never once needed a reason.

books.title: The Restorer's Secret
books.author: Celia Arkwright
books.blurb: Under a founder's portrait, a restorer finds a confession that could topple the valley's richest family.
pages: The portrait arrives at Ines Varga's studio in a crate stencilled with the Halloran crest, escorted by two men who do not take off their coats. Augustus Halloran, founder of the Halloran mills, painted in 1871: a stern man in black, one hand on a ledger, the other on a map of the river valley his family still owns. The varnish has gone the colour of strong tea. The family wants him bright again by the spring gala.

The man who signs the delivery papers is called Corwin Pell. He is the family's lawyer, though he says the word as if it were only one of several. He tells Ines the fee is generous, the deadline firm, and that Mrs Constance Halloran, the founder's great-great-granddaughter, takes a personal interest.

The Hallorans, he adds, value discretion above everything. Ines says that discretion is most of her job. She means it, at the time.

She works the way she always does: a square inch at a time, with swabs and solvent and a magnifying visor, lifting a century of grime and yellow varnish from the paint beneath. Augustus emerges slowly. A cold eye, a pink knuckle, a silver watch chain.

In the third week she takes the canvas to the infrared camera, routine for a painting of this age, to look for the artist's underdrawing. What she finds is handwriting.

It sits beneath the ledger in the founder's hand, painted over and invisible to the eye: four lines of careful script, laid down in carbon black on the bare ground before the portrait was begun. The infrared reads straight through the paint above it. Ines enlarges the image on her screen and reads it once, then again, while the radiator ticks in the cold studio.

I, Lydia Halloran, painted this portrait. Not Mr Faraday.

The rest she copies into her notebook word for word. My husband did not buy the river land. He forged the signature of Tobias Crane upon the deed, and I watched him do it. I have no voice in this house, so I have put the truth where he will look at it every day and never see it. Let whoever finds it be braver than I was.

It is signed, and dated, and witnessed by no one.

Ines knows the name Crane. Everyone in the valley does. The Cranes were the farming family who lost everything to the mills, and whose descendants still live in the town below them, in houses that flood every few winters because the Halloran weirs were built to spare the mills and not the street.

She sits for a long time looking at the screen. Then she saves the images in three places, and switches off the studio lights.

Two days later, Corwin Pell visits unannounced. He admires the work. He asks, lightly, whether she has used any special imaging on the painting, and whether she has found anything of note. Only the artist's sketch, Ines says. Very ordinary.

He smiles and says that is good to hear. On his way out he pauses by her computer, which is switched off, and rests two fingers on its lid, as though taking its temperature.

That night someone tries her studio door. She hears the handle turn, slowly, and then the soft scrape of a tool at the lock, and she stands in the dark at the top of the stairs with her phone in her hand, not breathing. The alarm she fitted the day before begins to wail. Footsteps hurry away down the lane.

In the morning there are fresh scratches round the keyhole, and her bins have been gone through.

Pell telephones at nine to say that the family has reconsidered. They would like the portrait returned at once, as it is. The fee will be paid in full, with a bonus for her trouble, in exchange for her signature on a short confidentiality agreement.

It is a very large bonus. Ines says she needs a day to make the painting safe for travel. Pell agrees, in a voice that suggests he is counting the hours.

She does not expect the second call. It comes from a private number in the afternoon, and the voice is old and clipped and tired. This is Constance Halloran, it says. I believe you've met my great-great-grandmother.

Ines goes cold. The old woman goes on. Her family has whispered about Lydia for a century, she says. She chose Ines because her reputation said she couldn't be bought. Was she right?

Constance explains the rest quickly, as if she has rehearsed it. Her son Julian runs the estate now, and Pell answers to him. Julian means to sell the river land to developers within the year, and a cloud on the title would cost him millions. Constance is eighty-seven. She cannot stop him alone.

But at the gala, she says, the portrait will be unveiled in front of the whole county. Is there a way to let Lydia speak?

There is. Ines spends the night building it: a narrow frame of infrared lamps to hang above the easel, and a small camera feeding the large screen the gala planners have already ordered for the slideshow. Under ordinary light the portrait will show only Augustus. Under the lamps, on the screen, Lydia's four lines will rise through the paint.

She returns the painting at noon, as promised, with the frame wrapped beside it.

The ballroom is full of candlelight and money. Julian Halloran gives a speech about heritage. Pell stands by the wall, watching Ines, and when Constance rises on her stick to unveil the portrait he steps towards the light switches.

He is too slow. Constance nods. Ines presses the switch in her pocket. The lamps hum, the screen flickers, and above the founder's ledger, in tall pale letters, a dead woman's handwriting appears.

The room goes very quiet. Then it goes very loud. Julian demands the screen be turned off, Pell demands Ines's camera, and three hundred guests, many of them holding telephones of their own, read the confession for themselves in the time it takes to argue.

By the time Pell reaches the plug, the images Ines sent that morning to the county archive, the land registry and the valley newspaper have already been opened.

The sale of the river land is halted by spring, and the title is in the courts by summer. Constance Halloran gives a third of her own share to a trust for the Crane families and the flooded street, and is said to have enjoyed the whole affair enormously.

The portrait hangs in the county museum now, restored and bright. The label beside it has been rewritten. It reads: Augustus Halloran, by Lydia Halloran, 1871.

Ines keeps one thing for herself: a print of the infrared image, framed above her workbench where she cannot help but see it every day. Beneath it she has copied out the last line in her own hand, as a reminder for the mornings when a fee is very large and a client's men do not take off their coats.

Let whoever finds it be braver than I was.

books.title: Line Two
books.author: Marguerite Osk
books.blurb: At three every morning the farmhouse phone rings, and someone on line two hums a familiar lullaby.
pages: The farmhouse came with the furniture, the chickens, and a black telephone on the hall table that the estate agent swore was disconnected. It was the old kind, heavy as a brick, with a rotary dial and two clear buttons along its base marked LINE ONE and LINE TWO. I liked it. I liked the whole place, its sagging porch and its orchard gone wild, and the way the hills folded round it like hands round a cup.

I had bought it with what my mother left me. She had died in the spring, quickly, the way she did everything, and I had spent the summer wanting to be somewhere nobody knew my face. The farm was three valleys from anyone. The nearest neighbour was a widower called Amos Kett, who brought me eggs I didn't need and told me nobody had lived in the house for thirty years.

The first night, the telephone rang at three in the morning.

I lay in bed and listened to it. It was a real bell, not a recording, a hard bright double ring that shook the house. I told myself it was a fault on the line, a mouse in the wires. On the ninth ring I went down in my socks, and the button marked LINE TWO was glowing a soft amber, like a coal in a grate.

I picked it up. I said hello.

Nobody answered. There was a hiss, like wind moving through long grass, and under it, very faint, somebody humming. A woman, I thought. Low and tuneless at first, and then finding the tune, and then I had to sit down on the stairs, because I knew it. Every note of it. My mother had hummed it over my bed every night until I was nine.

It wasn't a song you could buy. My mother told me once that her own mother made it up, though she never said much else about her. It went up three steps and down two, and the words, when there were words, were about a lamp in a window and a gate left open so the lambs could find their way home.

On the telephone, the humming finished. Then it began again from the start.

In the morning I unscrewed the wall plate in the hall. The wire for line one ran out under the porch to the pole on the road, and it had been cut cleanly years ago. The wire for line two went the other way. It ran along the skirting, through the kitchen, out by the back door and away up the hill behind the house, stapled to fence posts, towards the trees.

Amos Kett explained it when he came by with his eggs. In the old days, he said, there had been a shepherd's hut at the top of the hill pasture, and the family had strung a private line up to it for lambing time, so whoever sat up with the ewes could call down to the house.

He looked at the telephone for a long while. Then he said he'd best be off, and he forgot his basket.

It rang again that night, and the next, always at three. Always line two. Always the humming, patient and a little hoarse, as though the singer had a cold she was trying not to mention.

On the fourth night I didn't answer. I put on my boots and took a torch and followed the wire up the hill, fence post by fence post, while behind me in the dark house the telephone went on ringing.

The hut was still there, half swallowed by brambles, its iron wheels sunk in the turf. The door was open. Inside were a stove gone to rust, a bench, a lambing lamp on a hook, and on a shelf by the window a telephone exactly like mine. Its receiver was off the hook, lying on its side.

And I could still hear the ringing from the house below, though there was nobody up here to have called.

I found the rest in the parish records, in a cardboard box at the village hall that smelled of mice. A woman named Hester Lowe had lived at the farm with her husband and their baby daughter. One March a late snow came during lambing, and Hester went up to sit with the ewes. The drifts closed the hill for four days.

When they dug through to the hut, she was gone.

The baby's name was on the next line. It was my mother's name.

I read it three times. The child had been fostered, the record said, and then adopted two counties away. My mother never told me, and I don't think anyone ever told her. All she had kept of this place was a tune, carried in her the whole of her life, without knowing where it came from or who had hummed it first.

I could picture it. A young mother snowed in on a hill, frightened and feverish, lifting the receiver at three in the morning so that the baby crying in the house below would hear her and settle. Night after night, until she couldn't any more.

And then, I suppose, she kept on calling anyway. Because nobody had ever picked up the telephone and told her that it was all right to stop.

That night I sat on the stairs and waited. At three the bell rang and the amber light came on, and I lifted the receiver before the second ring. The humming started, tired and patient.

I said, She's grown, Hester. She grew up fine. She had a garden and a terrible laugh and a daughter of her own, and she sang her your song every night. I know all the words.

And then I sang it to her, down the line, the lamp and the gate and the lambs coming home, my voice cracking on the high step the way my mother's always had.

When I finished, the line was quiet. Not empty. Quiet, the way a room is quiet when someone has finally fallen asleep in it. I heard one long breath, like a sigh of relief. Then the amber light went out.

The telephone did not ring again for the rest of the autumn. I slept through the nights. Amos Kett started bringing his eggs in the mornings again, and staying for tea. Then, on the first night of the new year, it rang at three o'clock. Line two. I picked it up with my heart in my mouth, and there was the song, the lamp and the gate.

But this time there were two voices humming it.

books.title: The Keeper of Skerry Light
books.author: Fen Halloway
books.blurb: Cut off by a storm with three smugglers, a lighthouse keeper has only her light to call for help.
pages: Keeper's log, Skerry Light. Tuesday, 18:00. Wind south-west, force six and rising. Barometer falling fast. Lamp lit at 16:42, character correct: two white flashes every fifteen seconds. Relief boat postponed until the weather clears, which the mainland says will be Friday at the earliest. Stores ample. Generator sound. The gannets have all gone round to the lee side of the rock. They know something I don't. Signed, M. Toal, keeper.

Tuesday, 21:30. Force eight now, gusting nine. Spray reaching the gallery glass, sixty feet up. I note this for the record, and because there is nobody here to complain to but the log.

A vessel sighted at 21:10, showing no lights, running in towards the north cove, where no boat should ever come in weather like this. I have tried the radio twice. Nothing but a roar. I will go down and look.

Tuesday, 23:00. I went down as far as the old boathouse wall and lay flat in the heather with the binoculars. A fishing boat with her name painted out, rolling badly, tied up at the derelict jetty. Three men working by a red torch, passing crates up the slip. Heavy crates, sealed in plastic. Nobody lands cargo on a skerry in a gale unless they very much want nobody to see them doing it.

Wednesday, 01:15. The boat has gone. She cast off at half past midnight and lost her mooring line almost at once, and the sea took her round the point. I do not know if she made the open water.

The men did not go with her. I watched them carry the last crate into the boathouse. Then the tall one looked up at the tower, at my light going round, and started up the path.

Wednesday, 01:40. They are in the kitchen. I am writing this in the lamp room with the door bolted, in the minutes they have allowed me for my rounds.

The tall one calls himself Brannock. He was polite, which was worse. He says nobody need be hurt. He says the storm has stranded us all together, and when it lifts a bigger ship will come for them and their crates, and I will have seen nothing.

Wednesday, 02:30. Brannock has taken the radio handset and the batteries for the emergency beacon. The other two are brothers, I think: Sully, and the young one they call Pip, who looks green with seasickness and keeps apologising for the mud on my floor.

They need the light. Brannock said so. Their ship is coming in on my beam on Friday night, to find the north cove in the dark.

Wednesday, 11:00. Force ten. The radio mast came down in the night with a noise like a gunshot, so the handset would have done me no good anyway. We are truly cut off now.

I have kept to my routine, which Brannock allows, because the light matters to him. I wound the clockwork. I polished the lens. I trimmed the reserve lamp. And as I worked, I began to think about the lens.

For the record, for whoever reads this. Every lighthouse has its own character, its own pattern of flashes, so that a sailor at night can tell one light from another. Skerry's is two white flashes every fifteen seconds. It is printed on every chart for a hundred miles.

If Skerry ever shows anything else, the coastguard station on Carrick Head will know at once that something out here is wrong.

Wednesday, 23:00. Brannock watches me in the lamp room. He does not understand the machinery and he knows it, which makes him careful. I explained the clockwork to him at great length and very slowly, until he got bored and went down for his tea.

The lens turns on a bath of mercury, with screens between its panels. One screen is meant to be lifted out for cleaning. I have not put it back.

Thursday, 04:00. Skerry Light now shows three white flashes every fifteen seconds. To a man who has never read a chart, it looks exactly the same as before.

Pip came up at dawn with a mug of tea for me, of his own accord, and stood watching the beam go round. He said it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. I said yes, it is. I do not think he is cut out for this work.

Thursday, 15:00. The wind is easing. Brannock is restless and keeps going out on the gallery with his binoculars, looking for his ship. Sully counts the crates in the boathouse again and again.

I found Pip in the kitchen reading the old logs from the shelf, keepers' entries going back to 1890. He asked me if anyone had ever needed rescuing out here. I told him quite a few people, over the years.

Thursday, 22:10. Lights to the north-east. Not the ship Brannock was waiting for. A smaller vessel, moving fast and steady, and ahead of her the long white sweep of a searchlight on the water.

Brannock came up the stairs three at a time. He asked me what I had done. I told him the truth, which was that I had kept the light. He didn't understand. I don't think he ever will.

Thursday, 23:50. The coastguard cutter from Carrick Head is in the north cove, and the island is full of torches and voices. They saw the wrong light on Wednesday morning and set out the moment the sea would let them.

Brannock ran for the boathouse and found two officers already there. Sully gave himself up on the path. Pip was sitting on the kitchen step with his hands in the air before anyone asked him.

Friday, 09:00. The crates held counterfeit banknotes, near enough a ship's worth, bound for the mainland in time for the winter trade. The coastguard captain says the ship meant to collect them was stopped at sea at dawn, holding a course straight for my beam.

He asked how I had known to change the light. I said that it is a keeper's job to tell ships the truth, and I had only done my job.

Friday, 16:40. Wind north-west, force three. Barometer rising. Relief boat expected tomorrow with stores and post. Pip asked the captain to tell me he was sorry, and that he would like to read about lighthouses properly one day. I have sent him the spare copy of the keepers' manual.

Screen replaced. Lamp lit at 16:38. Character correct: two white flashes every fifteen seconds. The gannets are back. Signed, M. Toal, keeper.
